title: CPSC 541 - Chapter 1: The Essential Software Requirement

questions.question: According to Chapter 1, what is one of the biggest causes of software project failure?
options: Failure to understand and control requirements
questions.explanation: The chapter emphasizes that failure to understand and control requirements is a major cause of project failure.

questions.question: Why is discovering a requirements defect early so important?
options: Requirements cannot be changed after programming begins
Customers are not allowed to change their minds
The cost of correcting a defect generally increases the later it is discovered
Late defects can only be corrected by managers
questions.explanation: A requirements error discovered during requirements work is much cheaper to fix than one discovered during design, implementation, testing, or maintenance.

questions.question: Frederick Brooks argued that the hardest part of building a software system is deciding precisely what to build.
questions.explanation: Chapter 1 uses Brooks's observation to emphasize the importance and difficulty of requirements.

questions.question: Why can requirements engineering involve significant communication difficulty?
options: Only developers are allowed to define requirements
Requirements are created automatically from source code
Many different stakeholders can have different needs, priorities, and assumptions
Requirements are written after the product is released
questions.explanation: Customers, users, analysts, developers, testers, managers, legal staff, support staff, and others may all influence requirements.

questions.question: Which of the following are shortcomings that can occur during requirements gathering? Select all that apply.
options: Casual changes that are not properly recorded
questions.explanation: The first five can cause requirements problems. Maintaining a controlled baseline is a good requirements management practice.

questions.question: Which statement best describes a software requirement?
options: A description of the source code that developers must write
A specification of what should be implemented, including behavior, properties, attributes, or constraints
A schedule showing when programmers should finish
A testing script written after development
A diagram showing the final database tables
A list of programming languages approved by developers
questions.explanation: Requirements describe what should be implemented, how the system should behave, properties it must possess, or constraints it must respect.

questions.question: Which statement is closest to the formal IEEE-style meaning of a requirement presented in the chapter?
options: A programming technique selected by a developer
A condition or capability needed by a user to solve a problem or achieve an objective
A design pattern recommended by an architect
A testing method selected by quality assurance
A feature that developers personally believe would be useful
A project schedule approved by management
questions.explanation: The slides describe a requirement as a condition or capability needed by a user or one that a system must meet.

questions.question: A functional requirement primarily describes:
options: How much the project will cost
Which developer will implement a feature
A behavior the system will exhibit under specific conditions
How the development team will communicate
questions.explanation: Functional requirements describe system behavior under specified conditions.

questions.question: A system shall lock a user's account after three consecutive failed login attempts. What does this statement primarily describe?
questions.explanation: It specifies behavior the system must perform when a particular condition occurs.

questions.question: Which statement best describes a nonfunctional requirement?
options: A requirement that does not need to be implemented
A description of a property, characteristic, quality, or constraint the system must satisfy
A requirement written by someone other than a programmer
A feature removed from the project
A requirement that applies only to testing
A requirement that has not yet been approved
questions.explanation: Nonfunctional requirements describe characteristics such as performance, availability, security, usability, and constraints.

questions.question: A web application shall respond to user requests within two seconds under normal operating load. What kind of requirement is this?
questions.explanation: Response time describes performance, which is a quality attribute and therefore a type of nonfunctional requirement.

questions.question: Which of the following are examples of quality attributes? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Performance, availability, security, usability, and robustness are quality attributes. Project budget is not a software quality attribute.

questions.question: A constraint primarily does what?
options: Defines the business value of the project
Restricts the choices available to developers when designing or constructing the system
questions.explanation: A constraint limits the design or implementation choices available to the development team.

questions.question: Which information generally should NOT be placed in the software product requirements specification unless it represents a genuine constraint?
questions.explanation: Requirements should focus primarily on what must be built rather than detailed design, implementation, project planning, or test procedures.

questions.question: A business requirement primarily explains:
options: Exactly how a button should be programmed
Why the organization wants the product and what business objective it hopes to achieve
How testers should execute test cases
How a database table should be indexed
Which developer is responsible for a feature
Which programming language must be learned
questions.explanation: Business requirements express high-level business objectives, vision, and desired outcomes.

questions.question: A company wants its new self-service system to reduce customer-support calls by 30 percent. What type of requirement is this?
questions.explanation: This describes the business outcome the organization hopes the system will help achieve.

questions.question: A user requirement primarily describes:
options: A goal or task that a user must be able to accomplish with the system
The source code required to implement a feature
questions.explanation: User requirements describe goals, tasks, or desired product attributes from the user's perspective.

questions.question: Which ordering correctly represents the general relationship among the three major levels of requirements?
options: Functional requirements → user requirements → business requirements
User requirements → business requirements → functional requirements
Business requirements → user requirements → functional requirements
Functional requirements → business requirements → user requirements
System requirements → testing requirements → business requirements
Business requirements → source code → user requirements
questions.explanation: Business requirements explain why, user requirements describe what users need to accomplish, and functional requirements specify system behavior that supports those user tasks.

questions.question: A feature and a functional requirement are always the same thing.
questions.explanation: A feature can contain one or more logically related capabilities and can be described by multiple functional requirements.

questions.question: Requirements engineering is divided into which two major areas?
questions.explanation: Chapter 1 divides requirements engineering into requirements development and requirements management.

questions.question: Which four activities make up requirements development?
questions.explanation: Requirements development consists of elicitation, analysis, specification, and validation.

questions.question: A business analyst interviews employees to identify user classes, understand their tasks, and discover what they need from a new system. Which requirements activity is taking place?
questions.explanation: Elicitation is the process of discovering requirements and understanding users, their tasks, goals, and business objectives.

questions.question: During which requirements development activity would an analyst separate user goals, functional requirements, quality expectations, business rules, suggestions, and irrelevant information?
questions.explanation: Analysis involves organizing, refining, decomposing, prioritizing, and distinguishing the different kinds of information gathered.

questions.question: An analyst converts discovered user needs into organized written requirements and diagrams that developers and customers can review. Which activity is this?
questions.explanation: Specification means documenting the collected requirements knowledge in an organized and persistent form.

questions.question: A team reviews documented requirements with users to make sure everyone has the same understanding and to find errors before implementation begins. Which activity is this?
questions.explanation: Validation confirms that the documented requirements accurately represent what is needed before development proceeds.

questions.question: What is a requirements baseline?
options: The first rough idea discussed by a developer
A snapshot of the reviewed and agreed-upon set of requirements at a particular point in time
A list of all rejected requirements
A copy of the source code before testing
A document containing only business requirements
The minimum performance level of the software
questions.explanation: A baseline represents the current agreement about the requirements and provides a controlled starting point for managing changes.

questions.question: Which activities belong to requirements management? Select all that apply.
options: Defining and maintaining a requirements baseline
Evaluating the impact of proposed changes
Incorporating approved changes in a controlled way
Tracing requirements to design, code, and tests
Tracking requirement status and change activity
questions.explanation: Requirements management controls and tracks the agreed requirements and their changes. Changes should be evaluated rather than automatically accepted.

questions.question: A customer requests an additional feature after the requirements baseline has been established. What should the team do first?
options: Reject it because requirements can never change
Evaluate the proposed change and determine its impact before approving it
Wait until after deployment to consider it
Allow the developer who received the request to decide privately
questions.explanation: Requirements management allows change, but changes should be evaluated for effects on cost, schedule, design, code, testing, and other requirements.

questions.question: What is gold plating?
options: Giving the most important requirement the highest priority
Adding functionality that was not required because a developer believes the customer will like it
Improving the wording of an ambiguous requirement
Reviewing a requirement with multiple users
questions.explanation: Gold plating occurs when developers add unnecessary or unrequested functionality, which can consume time and money without delivering needed value.

questions.question: Which problems can result from ambiguous requirements? Select all that apply.
options: Different stakeholders interpret the same requirement differently
Developers may implement the wrong behavior
Testers and developers may have different expectations
Time can be wasted resolving misunderstandings
Requirements automatically become easier to verify
Stakeholders may be surprised by the delivered system
questions.explanation: Ambiguity creates multiple interpretations and mismatched expectations, which often lead to rework and wasted effort.

questions.question: Which combination contains the characteristics of an excellent individual requirement emphasized in Chapter 1?
options: Complete, correct, feasible, necessary, prioritized, unambiguous, and verifiable
Short, technical, complex, detailed, coded, tested, and deployed
Cheap, fast, flexible, optional, visual, reusable, and automated
Documented, programmed, compiled, deployed, monitored, patched, and archived
Profitable, graphical, object-oriented, distributed, scalable, portable, and cloud-based
Approved, implemented, tested, deployed, maintained, replaced, and deleted
questions.explanation: The slides identify complete, correct, feasible, necessary, prioritized, unambiguous, and verifiable as important characteristics of excellent requirements.
